newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO rejects U.S. compromise on Israeli pullback.
newsitem.headline: PLO rejects U.S. compromise on Israeli pullback.

text.p: Palestinians on Thursday turned down a U.S. compromise date for Israeli troop withdrawals in the West Bank, insisting Washington make Israel respect the original timetable.

The rejection was another blow to the Middle East peace mission of U.S. envoy Dennis Ross who has been shuttling for weeks between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Publicly, U.S. officials said Ross had no plans to return home but in private one official said he could leave on Friday if a meeting with Netanyahu late on Thursday drew a blank.
Arafat was also waiting for the outcome of Ross's meeting to determine whether he should leave for a scheduled European trip on Friday, PLO officials said.

Ross is trying to close a long-delayed deal on an Israeli withdrawal in Hebron. But Arafat, suspicious of Netanyahu's commitment to wider Palestinian self-rule, has been holding out for guaranteed dates for three further pullbacks in the rest of the West Bank.
"Israel has proposed to end the last stage of further redeployments from the rest of the West Bank in 1999. We rejected that," said Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, general secretary of the Palestinian presidency.
"So to break the deadlock in the talks Ross proposed as a compromise mid-1998, and we rejected this as well," he told Reuters.

"The Palestinian leadership will not make and cannot make any more compromises, especially on dates stated in the original agreement and the U.S. compromise is a violation of the deal that was signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton," Abdel-Rahim said.
Western diplomats said talks on extending Palestinian self-rule appeared bogged down.
"Both sides are now playing the blame game. There's not much more Ross can do for the moment," said one diplomat.

Both Netanyahu and Arafat accuse each other of delaying the talks. Negotiators say a deal on Hebron is all but reached. The argument now is over the timing and scope of three further redeployments which should be completed by September 7 this year under the Oslo peace accords.

Netanyahu, facing a revolt by as many as seven of his 18 cabinet ministers if he hands back Hebron, wants to extend redeployment into 1999, partly to strengthen his hand in talks on a final settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Arafat wants to be in control of the 90 percent of the West Bank he believes should be his under Oslo before negotiating such sensitive "final status" issues as Jerusalem, refugees and the powers of a Palestinian government.

"We cannot obviously abide by the dates as they are fixed in the agreement...because of the security situation deteriorating and because the Palestinian side has not been able and perhaps not been willing to do anything about it," Netanyahu's spokesman David Bar-Illan told Reuters.
Palestinian official Saeb Erekat said Ross held a "very positive" meeting with Arafat's senior aide Mahmoud Abbas on Thursday.
"Mr Ross will continue efforts with President Arafat and Prime Minister Netanyahu in the hope that the gaps will be bridged," Erekat told reporters

Palestinian officials said Ross listened more than he talked during the 2-1/2 hour meeting. Some Palestinian officials have been unusually critical of Ross in the past week, saying he is merely conveying Israel's positions.

Asked if Ross's mission had reached a dead end, Bar-Illan said: "I don't believe so. I think the Americans have contributed a great deal in facilitating efforts, and I think they should continue, simply for the one reason that they are the only power in the world today that has clout with both sides."
